title: Nana Asma'u
hookLine: the poet and scholar of Sokoto who trained women teachers across the region

lines: A TALL HAT ON THE ROAD.
cards: A woman sets out from her village on foot, wearing a tall, wide hat that marks her out on the road. She is walking to the city to learn.

There she will memorize a set of poems: about the Prophet, about prayer, about the women saints of Islam, about how to live. Then she will walk home, gather the women of her village, and teach them every line.

She is a jaji, a teacher. And the woman who trained her, who wrote many of those poems and sent teachers like her across the countryside, was the daughter of a reformer in what is now northern Nigeria. Today: Nana Asma'u.

teach.b: Nana Asma'u was the daughter of Shehu Usman dan Fodio, a scholar and reformer whose movement founded the Sokoto Caliphate in West Africa.
She grew up in a house full of books, learned the Qur'an by heart, and became a scholar in her own right.
She wrote poetry in Arabic and in the local languages, Fulfulde and Hausa, so that people who didn't read Arabic could still learn. Her problem was a practical one.
Women in the villages around Sokoto wanted to learn their faith, but they couldn't easily leave home and family for long. So she turned the problem around.

teach.h: THE JAJIS CARRY THE LESSONS HOME.
teach.b: Instead of bringing every woman to the city, she trained teachers, the jajis, who came to her, learned the lessons, and carried them back.
The women who gathered around them were called the yan taru, the ones who come together. And she wrote the lessons as poems, because a poem is easy to remember and easy to pass on by mouth.
Behind it all stood a simple conviction.
The Qur'an teaches a short prayer, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." And a hadith in Sunan Ibn Majah says that seeking knowledge is a duty on every Muslim.
Nana Asma'u took that duty to include the women of the villages. She could not teach them all.
She trained the teachers. Her poems are still recited in the region today.

how: In northern Nigeria, Nana Asma'u's poems are still recited, and women's study circles that trace themselves to her yan taru meet to learn together.

games.q: you're a scholar in Sokoto. women in the villages want to learn their faith, but they can't leave home for long. what do you do?
o: ask them to come to the city anyway.
train teachers who come to you and carry the lessons home in verse.
write one long book and hope it reaches them.
games.why: Nana Asma'u trained the jajis, who learned her poems by heart and taught the women of their villages, the yan taru.

practice: Bring to mind a woman or girl in your life, a daughter, a sister, a mother, a friend, and one small thing you know that she might want to know: something about faith, a skill, a recipe, a family story.
Think how you'd make it easy to remember, the way Nana Asma'u used verse. If you pray, ask that it reaches her well; if not, simply hold her in mind.
